source_text: Τοῦτον οὖν πρῶτον ἐπιγνῶναι τῷ ζησομένῳ τὴν ὄντως ζωὴν παρακελεύεται, ὃν »οὐδεὶς ἐπιγινώσκει εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱὸς καὶ ᾧ ἂν ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψῃ«. ἔπειτα τὸ μέγεθος τοῦ σωτῆρος μετ᾿ ἐκεῖνον καὶ τὴν καινότητα τῆς χάριτος μαθεῖν, ὅτι δὴ κατὰ τὸν ἀπόστολον »ὁ νόμος διὰ Μωσέως ἐδόθη, ἡ χάρις καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ«· καὶ οὐκ ἴσα τὰ διὰ δούλου πιστοῦ διδόμενα τοῖς ὑπὸ [τοῦ] υἱοῦ γνησίου δωρουμένοις. εἰ γοῦν ἱκανὸς ἦν ὁ Μωσέως νόμος ζωὴν αἰώνιον παρασχεῖν, μάτην μὲν ὁ σωτὴρ αὐτὸς παραγίνεται καὶ πάσχει δι᾿ ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ γενέσεως μέχρι τοῦ σημείου τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα διατρέχων, μάτην δὲ ὁ πάσας πεποιηκὼς »ἐκ νεότητος« τὰς νομίμους ἐντολὰς παρὰ ἄλλου αἰτεῖ γονυπετῶν ἀθανασίαν. οὐδὲ γὰρ πεπλήρωκε μόνον τὸν νόμον, ἀλλὰ καὶ εὐθὺς ἀπὸ πρώτης ἡλικίας ἀρξάμενος· ἐπεὶ καὶ τί μέγα ἢ ὑπέρλαμπρον γῆρας ἄγονον ἀδικημάτων ὧν ἐπιθυμίαι τίκτουσι νεανικαὶ ἢ ὀργὴ ζέουσα ἢ ἔρως χρημάτων; ἀλλ᾿ εἴ τις ἐν σκιρτήματι νεοτησίῳ καὶ τῷ καύσωνι τῆς ἡλικίας παρέσχηται φρόνημα πεπανὸν καὶ πρεσβύτερον τοῦ χρόνου, θαυμαστὸς οὗτος ἀγωνιστὴς καὶ διαπρεπὴς καὶ τὴν γνώμην πολιός. ἀλλ᾿ ὅμως οὗτος ὁ τοιοῦτος ἀκριβῶς πέπεισται, διότι αὐτῷ πρὸς μὲν δικαιοσύνην οὐδὲν ἐνδεῖ, ζωῆς δὲ ὅλως προσδεῖ· διὸ αὐτὴν αἰτεῖ παρὰ τοῦ δοῦναι μόνου δυναμένου· καὶ πρὸς μὲν τὸν νόμον ἄγει παρρησίαν, τοῦ θεοῦ δὲ τὸν υἱὸν ἱκετεύει. »ἐκ πίστεως εἰς πίστιν« μετατάσσεται· ὡς σφαλερῶς ἐν νόμῳ σαλεύων καὶ ἐπικινδύνως ναυλοχῶν εἰς τὸν σωτῆρα μεθορμίζεται.
thought_title: From the law to the Savior: the rich man's request for life
orientation: Clement is explaining what must be learned first for salvation, and now turns to the rich man's recognition that the law cannot give eternal life.
pass_a_gloss: This one, then, he urges first to know him who is to live the true life, whom 'no one knows except the Son and he to whom the Son may reveal him.' Then, after that one, to learn the greatness of the Savior and the newness of the grace, that indeed according to the apostle 'the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ'; and the things given through a faithful servant are not equal to the things bestowed by the genuine Son. If indeed the law of Moses had been sufficient to provide eternal life, in vain the Savior himself comes and suffers for us, running through humanity from birth to the sign, and in vain the one who has done all the lawful commandments 'from youth' asks from another, falling on his knees, for immortality. For he has not only fulfilled the law, but also having begun right from his first age; since what great or surpassing thing is an old age barren of wrongs which youthful desires or boiling anger or love of money beget? But if someone in the leaping of youth and the burning heat of his age has shown a mind ripe and older than his time, this one is a wondrous contestant and distinguished and gray in judgment. But nevertheless this one, such as he is, is precisely persuaded that for him nothing is lacking for righteousness, but he lacks life altogether; therefore he asks it from the only one able to give it; and toward the law he brings boldness, but he supplicates the Son of God. 'From faith to faith' he is transferred; as one swaying dangerously in the law and anchoring perilously, he moves to a new mooring in the Savior.

lemmas.gloss: he moves to a new mooring, changes anchorage

choices.why: The adverb ὄντως ('really, truly') modifies ζωήν; rendering as 'true life' preserves the emphatic sense of real, genuine life as opposed to mere existence.
The article before χάριτος makes it definite; keeping 'the grace' preserves the specific reference to the grace that came through Jesus Christ in the following quotation.
πιστοῦ is attributive to δούλου, describing Moses as faithful; the word order 'faithful servant' is natural English and keeps the adjective's force.
rejected: through a servant who was faithful

choices.why: γένεσις here means birth or origin, and σημεῖον likely refers to the cross or a specific point; rendering literally as 'the sign' preserves the source's compressed reference without over-interpreting.
rejected: from his birth to the cross

choices.why: σκίρτημα means a leap or bound, used metaphorically of youthful exuberance; 'leaping' keeps the vivid physical image rather than flattening it to 'vigor' or 'exuberance.'
πολιός literally means gray-haired; applied to γνώμη it means mature or wise in mind. 'Gray in judgment' preserves the metaphor of age applied to the mind.

bible_refs.note: οὐδεὶς ἐπιγινώσκει εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱὸς καὶ ᾧ ἂν ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψῃ
ὁ νόμος διὰ Μωσέως ἐδόθη, ἡ χάρις καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
ἐκ νεότητος (the rich man's claim to have kept the commandments from youth)

pass_b_english: So he urges the one who is to live the true life to know first of all him whom "no one knows except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him" (Matthew 11:27). Then, after him, he must learn the greatness of the Savior and the newness of the grace, because, as the apostle says, "the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ" (John 1:17). And the things given through a faithful servant are not equal to the things bestowed by the true-born Son.

If the law of Moses had been sufficient to provide eternal life, then the Savior would have come in vain and suffered in vain, running through our humanity from birth to the sign. And in vain would the man who had kept all the commandments of the law "from his youth" (Mark 10:20) kneel before another and ask for immortality. For he has not only fulfilled the law, but he did so beginning right from his earliest age. After all, what is so great or brilliant about an old age barren of the wrongs that youthful desires give birth to, or that boiling anger or love of money produce? But if someone in the leaping of youth and the burning heat of that age shows a mind ripe and older than his years, that man is a marvelous and distinguished athlete, gray in judgment.

And yet this man, for all that, is thoroughly convinced that he lacks nothing when it comes to righteousness, but that he is entirely lacking in life. That is why he asks for it from the only one who can give it. He approaches the law with confidence, but he begs the Son of God. He is moving "from faith to faith" (Romans 1:17); as one who rocks dangerously in the law and lies at anchor in peril, he changes his mooring to the Savior.

last_rejected.why: γνησίος means 'legitimate/true-born' but here contrasts with 'faithful servant'; 'genuine Son' better fits the contrast.
last_rejected.ruling: γνήσιος means genuine/authentic; 'true‑born' is odd but still conveys authenticity, not a change of meaning

last_rejected.why: Greek says "civic mind" (citizen's judgment), not a gray‑aged judgment.
last_rejected.ruling: πολιὸς means 'gray/gray-haired' (cf. LSJ); with γνῶμην it = 'gray in judgment.' Not from πολίτης 'citizen.'

polish.changed: Clarified the flow of the argument by breaking it into three paragraphs where the thought turns, made the subject of each sentence explicit, and smoothed the sentence order so the contrast between the law and the Savior, and the rich man's confidence before the law versus his begging before the Son, reads naturally aloud.

notes.quote: running through our humanity from birth to the sign
notes.why: 'The sign' is unexplained; likely refers to the sign of the cross or baptism.
notes.fix: Clarify: 'from birth to the cross' or 'to baptism.'
